name: Ad Hominem
short_definition: Attacking the person making an argument instead of actually responding to what they said.
full_explanation: An ad hominem fallacy happens when someone tries to dismiss an argument by pointing out something negative about the person who made it — like their age, appearance, past mistakes, or personality — rather than showing what's actually wrong with the argument itself. The problem is that who you are has nothing to do with whether your reasoning is correct. In debate, this often surfaces in crossfire when a debater says something like 'You can't trust their sources — they're biased!' without explaining what's actually wrong with the evidence.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Listen for attacks on the debater or their team instead of their arguments — phrases like 'Of course you'd say that' or 'Your team doesn't even understand the topic.' If the critique is about a person's character rather than the logic of what they said, it's ad hominem.
example_debate: Debater A argues that schools should start later for student health. Debater B replies, 'You're only saying that because you always come to school late anyway.' Debater B never actually addresses the health evidence — they just attack Debater A personally.
counter_response: Point out that your argument stands or falls on its own evidence, not on who you are — ask your opponent to address the actual claim.

name: Straw Man
short_definition: Twisting or exaggerating what someone said to make it easier to argue against.
full_explanation: The straw man fallacy occurs when a debater distorts their opponent's position into a weaker or more extreme version, then attacks that fake version as if they had refuted the real argument. Just like it's easy to knock over a dummy made of straw, it's easy to defeat an argument that was never actually made. In PF debate, this frequently shows up in crossfire when a debater mischaracterizes what their opponent's case actually said, then triumphantly tears down that distorted version.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Watch for phrases like 'So you're saying that...' followed by a claim your opponent never actually made. If the paraphrase sounds more extreme or absurd than what was argued, it's likely a straw man.
example_debate: Debater A argues for requiring students to wear helmets during certain school sports. Debater B responds, 'My opponents think students can't make any decisions for themselves and want the school to control everything students do.' That's not what Debater A said — it's a distorted, extreme version.
counter_response: Correct the record immediately: 'That's not what we argued — our actual position is [X], please respond to that.'

name: Red Herring
short_definition: Changing the subject to something unrelated to distract from the real issue.
full_explanation: A red herring is when a debater introduces an irrelevant topic or argument to steer the conversation away from the actual issue being debated. The name comes from the idea of dragging a smelly fish across a trail to throw off hunting dogs. In crossfire, this tactic can be deliberate or accidental — a debater might bring up an interesting but off-topic point to avoid answering a tough question or to muddy the waters around their opponent's strong argument.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Notice when a response takes the conversation to a completely different topic instead of answering the question asked. If you're debating climate policy and your opponent starts talking about something unrelated to the resolution, that's a red herring.
example_debate: Debater A asks, 'What evidence do you have that your economic policy works?' Debater B answers, 'Well, what we really should be talking about is how unfair it is that some schools get so much more funding than others.' Debater B changed the subject entirely instead of answering.
counter_response: Call it out directly: 'That doesn't answer my question — I'm asking about [the original topic], please address that.'

name: False Dichotomy
short_definition: Presenting only two choices when there are actually more options available.
full_explanation: The false dichotomy fallacy forces people to choose between only two options as if no other possibilities exist, when in reality there are many more alternatives. It creates a fake 'all or nothing' situation to pressure people into accepting one side. In debate, this shows up when a debater claims 'either you support our policy, or you want the problem to get worse' — ignoring the many other possible approaches to the issue.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Listen for 'either...or' framing, or absolute statements that suggest only two outcomes are possible. Ask yourself: are there really only two options here?
example_debate: Debater A says, 'Either we ban all junk food in school cafeterias, or we're choosing to harm students' health.' In reality, there are many middle-ground options — like offering healthier choices alongside current ones, or nutrition education — that Debater A is ignoring.
counter_response: Identify the middle ground: 'That's a false choice — there are many other options we haven't considered, like [alternative].'

name: Slippery Slope
short_definition: Claiming that one small step will automatically lead to a chain of extreme, bad outcomes without showing why each step would actually happen.
full_explanation: The slippery slope fallacy argues that if we allow one thing to happen, it will inevitably set off a chain reaction ending in a terrible result — but without providing evidence that each step in that chain is actually likely. It's not always wrong to worry about where something leads, but the fallacy occurs when the path from A to Z is just assumed rather than shown. In PF crossfire, debaters sometimes use this to make opponents' policies sound catastrophic without real evidence of the chain of events.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Look for a chain of 'and then... and then... and then...' logic where each step is assumed but never backed up with evidence. The more extreme the endpoint compared to the starting policy, the more likely it's a slippery slope.
example_debate: Debater A argues for a small increase in the school dress code. Debater B responds, 'If we give the school this power, next they'll control what students eat, then what students read, and eventually students will have no freedom at all.' No evidence is given for why any of those steps would actually happen.
counter_response: Challenge the links: 'You need to show evidence that each step in that chain would actually happen — just claiming it doesn't make it true.'

name: Appeal to Authority
short_definition: Using someone's opinion as proof just because they are famous or seem important, even if they are not actually an expert on the topic.
full_explanation: It's perfectly fine to cite real experts in a debate — in fact, that's what good evidence looks like. The fallacy occurs when the 'authority' cited is not actually an expert in the relevant field (like a celebrity endorsing a medical claim), or when authorities in the field genuinely disagree but only one side is mentioned. In PF crossfire, debaters sometimes quote a public figure or organization without checking whether that source has relevant expertise or whether their quote was taken out of context.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Ask: is this person actually an expert in this specific area? Is this authority relevant to the claim being made? Are there other experts who disagree? If the answer to any of these raises doubt, the appeal may be fallacious.
example_debate: Debater A argues that a new social media policy is bad by saying, 'A famous actor tweeted that this policy is dangerous, so it must be.' An actor's opinion on policy — with no cited expertise — is not reliable evidence.
counter_response: Ask about the source's actual qualifications: 'What makes this person an expert on this specific issue? Do experts in the field actually agree?'

name: Appeal to Emotion
short_definition: Using strong feelings like pity, fear, or excitement to persuade people instead of using actual evidence and logic.
full_explanation: Emotional appeals are powerful and are often used in debate to help listeners connect with an argument — and that can be legitimate when emotions are backed by facts. The fallacy occurs when emotion is used as a substitute for evidence rather than a supplement to it. In PF crossfire, this can appear when a debater tries to shut down questioning by saying something like 'how can you argue against this when people are suffering?' without addressing the logical merits of the case.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Notice when a response relies entirely on how something makes people feel, without any evidence or reasoning. If removing the emotional language would leave the argument empty, it's likely a fallacious appeal.
example_debate: Debater A asks for evidence that a policy will be effective. Debater B responds, 'I can't believe you'd question this — think about all the children who are hurting right now.' The emotional framing avoids answering the question about effectiveness.
counter_response: Acknowledge the concern while redirecting: 'We understand this is an important issue, but we need to focus on whether the evidence shows the policy actually works.'

name: Appeal to Ignorance
short_definition: Claiming something must be true because nobody has proven it false, or claiming something is false because nobody has proven it true.
full_explanation: This fallacy confuses the absence of evidence with evidence of absence (or presence). Just because something hasn't been disproven doesn't mean it's true, and just because something hasn't been proven doesn't mean it's false. In PF crossfire, this often surfaces as a burden of proof issue — one side might say 'You can't prove our policy will fail, so it must work!' without providing any positive evidence that it will succeed.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Listen for claims that hinge on what hasn't been proven: 'There's no proof it's harmful' used as if that means it's definitely safe, or 'Nobody has disproved our plan' used as evidence the plan works.
example_debate: Debater A argues for a new climate policy. Debater B responds, 'Scientists haven't been able to predict exactly when the effects will hit, so we can't say climate change is as bad as they claim.' The inability to pinpoint an exact date doesn't mean the broader scientific consensus is wrong.
counter_response: Clarify the burden: 'The absence of disproof is not the same as proof — what positive evidence supports your claim?'

name: Bandwagon
short_definition: Arguing that something must be right or true just because a lot of people believe it or do it.
full_explanation: The bandwagon fallacy confuses popularity with correctness. The fact that many people believe something — or that a trend is growing — doesn't make it true or good. Throughout history, majorities have held wrong or harmful views. In PF debate, this fallacy pops up when a debater argues that a policy is good simply because it's gaining public support, or that an opponent's position is wrong because it's unpopular.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Watch for phrases like 'most people agree,' 'polls show everyone supports this,' or 'that position is out of touch with public opinion' used as the primary reason to accept a claim rather than as one piece of evidence.
example_debate: Debater A says, 'Our policy on social media regulation must be correct — surveys show 70% of Americans support more regulation.' But popularity doesn't prove that a specific regulation will be effective or well-designed.
counter_response: Redirect to evidence: 'Popularity doesn't prove effectiveness — what evidence shows this policy actually solves the problem?'

name: Circular Reasoning
short_definition: Using your conclusion as one of your reasons, so your argument just goes in a circle without actually proving anything.
full_explanation: Circular reasoning happens when the conclusion of an argument is quietly assumed in one of its own premises. The argument looks like it's proving something, but it's really just restating the same idea in different words. In crossfire, this can be subtle — a debater might defend their case by saying essentially 'our policy is good because good policies like ours achieve great results,' which assumes what needs to be proven.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: If you strip away the fancy language, are the premise and the conclusion saying the same thing? If asking 'but why?' to the main premise just brings you back to the conclusion, that's circular.
example_debate: Debater A claims, 'We should trust the government to regulate the internet because the government is a trustworthy regulator.' The claim that the government is trustworthy is exactly what was supposed to be proven in the first place.
counter_response: Ask for independent evidence: 'That's circular — your reason for the conclusion is just restating the conclusion. What independent evidence supports this?'

name: Hasty Generalization
short_definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from only a few examples that may not represent the whole picture.
full_explanation: A hasty generalization takes a small number of cases — or even a single example — and treats them as if they represent everyone or everything. The conclusion might happen to be true, but the reasoning is weak because the sample is too small or too limited. In PF debate, this often appears when a debater uses one or two isolated examples as if they prove a general trend, without checking whether those examples are representative.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Ask: how many examples are being used to support this general claim? Are those examples typical, or could they be outliers? Phrases like 'students at one school showed...' used to make claims about 'all students' signal a hasty generalization.
example_debate: Debater A argues that all social media platforms are harmful to teens, citing two studies about one platform. Without showing whether these two studies represent the full range of platforms and research, the broad conclusion isn't supported.
counter_response: Challenge the sample size: 'Two examples aren't enough to prove a general trend — is there broader evidence that this holds across different contexts?'

name: Post Hoc
short_definition: Assuming that because one thing happened before another, the first thing must have caused the second.
full_explanation: Post hoc ergo propter hoc is Latin for 'after this, therefore because of this.' Just because two events happen in sequence doesn't mean the first caused the second — there could be a totally different cause, or it could just be a coincidence. In PF debate, this is very common when debaters argue that a policy caused an improvement (or a problem) just because the improvement (or problem) happened after the policy was introduced, without showing a real causal mechanism.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Watch for arguments structured as 'Policy X was passed, then outcome Y happened, therefore X caused Y.' Ask: could there be another explanation? Was there a real causal link established, or just a timeline?
example_debate: Debater A argues, 'After our city started a new recycling program, littering decreased by 30% — so recycling programs reduce littering.' But many other things could have happened at the same time (new laws, public campaigns, seasonal changes) that actually caused the drop in littering.
counter_response: Challenge the causal link: 'Happening at the same time or in sequence isn't the same as causing — what evidence shows a direct causal connection?'

name: Correlation vs. Causation
short_definition: Mistaking the fact that two things happen together for proof that one of them causes the other.
full_explanation: A correlation means two things tend to occur together or move in the same direction — but that doesn't mean one causes the other. Both might be caused by a third factor (a 'confounding variable'), or the pattern could be pure coincidence. In PF debate, this fallacy is especially common when discussing statistics: debaters may present a strong correlation as if it automatically proves causation without establishing a mechanism.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: When a debater uses statistics showing that two variables move together, ask: is there a real explanation for why one would cause the other, or could there be a third factor at work? Could the relationship be a coincidence?
example_debate: Debater A says, 'Countries with more social media users have higher rates of anxiety in teens, which proves social media causes anxiety.' But both could be caused by a third factor — like a general rise in screen time across all tech, or economic stress — rather than social media itself.
counter_response: Ask for the mechanism: 'A correlation doesn't prove causation — what is the causal mechanism, and have other explanations been ruled out?'

name: Tu Quoque
short_definition: Defending yourself or your argument by pointing out that your opponent does the same thing, instead of actually responding to the criticism.
full_explanation: Tu quoque is Latin for 'you too' or 'you also.' This fallacy deflects a valid criticism by pointing to the critic's own similar behavior or past statements. Even if the critic is a hypocrite, that doesn't make their argument wrong — hypocrisy is a character flaw, not a logical rebuttal. In crossfire, this shows up when a debater responds to a strong challenge by saying 'well, your side does this too' rather than addressing the substance.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: If a response to a criticism is entirely about what the questioner or their side has done, rather than addressing the actual argument, that's tu quoque. 'Your team's evidence also uses that same method!' doesn't address the critique.
example_debate: Debater A points out that Debater B's team used a statistic incorrectly. Debater B replies, 'Your team also misused a statistic in your first speech!' Even if that's true, it doesn't fix or excuse the original error.
counter_response: Acknowledge the parallel but return to the point: 'That's separate from the issue at hand — the question is whether your statistic is being used correctly.'

name: Equivocation
short_definition: Using the same word in two different senses during an argument to make it appear more convincing than it actually is.
full_explanation: Equivocation exploits words that have more than one meaning. An argument might use a word one way in the premise and a different way in the conclusion, making it seem logical when it isn't. This can be intentional (a rhetorical trick) or accidental. In PF crossfire, equivocation often sneaks in with key debate terms — words like 'freedom,' 'safe,' or 'effective' can mean different things in different contexts, and switching between meanings can make a weak argument look strong.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Pay close attention when a key term appears multiple times in an argument. Ask: is the word being used consistently, or does its meaning subtly shift? If different definitions are being used, call for clarification.
example_debate: Debater A argues, 'The law requires that all citizens have equal rights. Giving extra financial aid to lower-income students gives them extra rights. Therefore, this policy violates the law.' Here 'rights' shifts from legal rights to financial benefits — two very different meanings.
counter_response: Point out the ambiguity: 'You're using [word] in two different senses — can you clarify which definition you're using consistently throughout?'

name: Loaded Question
short_definition: Asking a question that sneaks in an unfair assumption, so that any answer seems to accept something that was never proven.
full_explanation: A loaded question embeds one or more unjustified assumptions into the question itself. No matter how you answer, you appear to accept those assumptions. This is a common debate and crossfire tactic because it puts opponents on the defensive immediately. In PF crossfire, loaded questions are used to get opponents to inadvertently concede a point they haven't actually agreed to.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Before answering any crossfire question, ask: what assumptions does this question contain? If answering 'yes' or 'no' would force you to accept something false, the question is loaded.
example_debate: During crossfire, Debater A asks, 'When did your side decide it was okay to ignore the economic impacts of your plan?' This question assumes Debater B's side has been ignoring economic impacts — which is the very point being debated.
counter_response: Reject the assumption before answering: 'That question assumes we ignored economic impacts, which we didn't — let me explain what our analysis actually shows.'

name: Burden of Proof Shifting
short_definition: Demanding that others prove you wrong instead of providing evidence for your own claim.
full_explanation: In debate, whoever makes a claim has the responsibility to provide evidence for it — that's the burden of proof. The fallacy occurs when a debater tries to shift that burden to their opponent, saying things like 'prove me wrong' rather than 'here's my evidence.' This is especially tricky in crossfire because it can be disguised as a reasonable challenge. According to pragma-dialectics (a formal framework for debate analysis), evading the burden of proof is a core violation of good argumentation.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Watch for responses that don't provide any evidence for a claim but instead challenge opponents to disprove it. 'You can't prove our policy won't work, so you have no reason to oppose it' shifts the burden inappropriately.
example_debate: Debater A claims a new technology will solve climate change. When challenged, Debater A says, 'You can't prove it won't work, so the burden is on you to show otherwise.' But Debater A made the original claim and should provide the evidence.
counter_response: Return the burden: 'You made the original claim, so the evidence responsibility is yours — what positive evidence shows this will work?'

name: Anecdotal Evidence
short_definition: Using one personal story or isolated example as if it proves a general rule, while ignoring larger bodies of data.
full_explanation: Personal stories are compelling and emotionally powerful, but a single example — even a true one — rarely proves a general claim. The anecdotal fallacy happens when someone treats their own experience or a vivid story as more reliable than systematic research. In PF debate, this shows up when a debater cites one person's experience to counter a statistical trend, or when a single news story is used as evidence for a widespread pattern.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: When an argument rests on phrases like 'I know someone who...' or a single story, ask whether this is being used as proof of a general trend rather than as illustration. Is there larger systematic evidence to support the claim?
example_debate: Debater A argues that standardized testing is ineffective, and cites a single student who scored high on tests but failed in college. One example doesn't reflect the performance of thousands of students and can't overturn studies tracking thousands of data points.
counter_response: Ask for systemic evidence: 'One case doesn't represent everyone — is there broader research that supports this claim across a larger population?'

name: Cherry Picking
short_definition: Only using evidence that supports your argument while ignoring data that contradicts it.
full_explanation: Cherry picking is the practice of selectively presenting evidence that supports one's position while intentionally or carelessly leaving out evidence that goes against it. Even if every piece of evidence cited is true, the overall picture is dishonest. This is one of the most common fallacies in PF debate because the research process naturally surfaces conflicting studies, and debaters may only include the ones that favor their case.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Ask whether there are conflicting studies or data points the other side hasn't mentioned. If the evidence presented seems one-sided, ask: 'Are there studies that found the opposite result? Why weren't those included?'
example_debate: Debater A argues that a particular educational policy dramatically improved test scores, citing three studies that found positive results — without mentioning the five larger studies that found no effect or mixed results.
counter_response: Challenge the completeness: 'Are there other studies on this topic? What do the studies that didn't support your conclusion say?'

name: No True Scotsman
short_definition: Changing the definition of a group or position after someone points out a counterexample, to protect your original claim from being disproven.
full_explanation: The No True Scotsman fallacy is a way of protecting a sweeping generalization by redefining terms whenever a counterexample is raised. Instead of accepting that the counterexample challenges the claim, the arguer declares that the counterexample 'doesn't count' as a true member of the group. This is a form of circular reasoning — the definition keeps shifting to keep the original claim safe. In crossfire, it appears when a debater constantly moves the goalposts when challenged with contrary evidence.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Listen for 'but that's not a real [X]' or 'that's not what we meant by [term]' whenever a counterexample is presented. If the definition keeps changing to exclude inconvenient cases, that's this fallacy.
example_debate: Debater A claims: 'No properly run government program has ever wasted money.' Debater B gives a counterexample. Debater A responds: 'Well, that wasn't a truly well-run program.' The definition of 'properly run' is being redefined on the fly to protect the original claim.
counter_response: Ask for a fixed definition upfront: 'Before you dismiss that example, define exactly what counts as [X] — and that definition shouldn't change when counterexamples arise.'

name: Appeal to Tradition
short_definition: Arguing that something is good or correct just because it's been done that way for a long time.
full_explanation: The appeal to tradition assumes that old practices are automatically better or more valid than new ideas. While tradition can sometimes provide relevant context, it is not itself proof that something is correct or beneficial — many harmful practices have long histories. In PF debate, this fallacy appears when a debater opposes reform by saying 'we've always done it this way' without showing why the old way actually works better.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Look for arguments where 'we've always done this,' 'this has been the practice for years,' or similar historical references are offered as the primary reason to continue a policy, without any functional or empirical support.
example_debate: Debater A argues against changing the school schedule by saying, 'Schools have always started at 7:30 AM — there's no good reason to change something that has worked for decades.' The long history of the policy doesn't by itself prove it's optimal or backed by evidence.
counter_response: Distinguish history from evidence: 'The fact that something has been done for a long time doesn't prove it's the best approach — what evidence shows it still works better than the alternative?'

name: Appeal to Nature
short_definition: Arguing that something is good or right just because it is natural, or bad because it is 'unnatural.'
full_explanation: The appeal to nature falsely treats 'natural' as synonymous with 'good,' 'safe,' or 'correct,' and 'unnatural' as synonymous with 'bad.' In reality, many natural things are harmful (arsenic, certain diseases) and many artificial things are beneficial (vaccines, clean drinking water). In debate, this fallacy is used to oppose new technologies or policies by labeling them 'unnatural' without providing real evidence of harm.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Notice when 'natural' or 'unnatural' is used as the main argument for or against something, without empirical evidence about actual effects. Ask: does being natural actually make it better or safer in this context?
example_debate: Debater A argues against genetically modified crops by saying, 'Changing the genes of food crops is unnatural — nature designed these plants a certain way, and we shouldn't interfere.' Whether something is natural says nothing about whether it is safe, effective, or beneficial.
counter_response: Challenge the logic: 'Natural doesn't automatically mean good or safe — what specific evidence shows this is harmful or beneficial, beyond the natural/unnatural label?'

name: False Analogy
short_definition: Comparing two things as if they are similar when they are actually different in ways that matter for the argument.
full_explanation: Analogies are useful tools in debate — they help explain complex ideas using familiar examples. A false analogy breaks down when the two things being compared are actually significantly different in ways that affect the conclusion. In PF crossfire, debaters sometimes use catchy analogies that sound convincing but fall apart when examined because the comparison doesn't hold up where it counts.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: When an opponent uses an analogy, ask: are these two things actually similar in the relevant way? What important differences might make the analogy break down?
example_debate: Debater A argues for stricter gun background checks by comparing gun purchases to driver's licenses: 'We require licenses to drive, so we should require licenses to buy guns.' While the analogy is useful, it breaks down in several ways — the legal framework, constitutional context, and existing regulations for cars vs. guns differ significantly.
counter_response: Point out the relevant difference: 'That analogy breaks down because [specific key difference] — the situations aren't comparable in the way that matters here.'

name: Affirming the Consequent
short_definition: Incorrectly concluding that because a result happened, a specific cause must be true — when other causes are possible.
full_explanation: This formal fallacy has the structure: 'If A then B. B is true. Therefore A must be true.' This is invalid because B could be caused by many things besides A. Just because the expected result happened doesn't mean the assumed cause is what produced it. In PF debate, this appears when a debater points to a positive outcome and assumes their favored policy must be the reason for it, without ruling out other explanations.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Watch for reasoning that goes: 'We predicted [outcome] if [policy], and [outcome] happened, so our policy must have worked.' Other factors could explain the outcome.
example_debate: Debater A argues: 'Our economic model predicts job growth when taxes are cut. Jobs grew after the tax cut. So the tax cut caused the job growth.' But jobs could have grown for many reasons — a growing economy, technological changes, demographic shifts — that had nothing to do with the tax cut.
counter_response: Challenge the causal assumption: 'The conclusion doesn't follow — B could be true for many reasons other than A. What rules out those alternatives?'

name: Denying the Antecedent
short_definition: Incorrectly concluding that because a condition is not met, the result cannot happen — when the result could still happen another way.
full_explanation: This formal fallacy has the structure: 'If A then B. A is not true. Therefore B is not true.' This is invalid because B could still be caused by other things. Just because one sufficient condition for a result is absent doesn't mean the result is impossible. In PF debate, this comes up when debaters argue that because a policy was not implemented, a good (or bad) outcome definitely cannot occur — ignoring other pathways.
how_to_spot_in_crossfire: Watch for 'If we don't do X, then Y can't happen' arguments — the absence of one pathway doesn't close off all others.
example_debate: Debater A argues: 'Only if we implement this recycling program will environmental waste decrease. We're not implementing this program. Therefore environmental waste will not decrease.' But waste might decrease through other policies — consumer behavior changes, different regulations, or industry innovation.
counter_response: Point out alternative pathways: 'Even without that condition, the outcome could still happen — what about [alternative cause]?'
